neighbours.label: Fires on a noun naming a group of people treated as a population whose outcomes are measured or compared (graduates, teenagers, residents, age groups), not on nouns for things counted in the same kind of statistic.
fire: Two-thirds of the college's alumni found jobs within six months.
The study found that today's retirees save less than their parents did.
Nearly half of the town's voters stayed home on election day.
Polls suggest that younger graduates are more likely to rent than buy.
Researchers compared how many immigrants and natives start small businesses.
Only 12 percent of the district's pupils passed the advanced exam.
The report shows that rural households spend more on fuel than urban ones.
Surveys suggest that most smokers want to quit within a year.
quiet: Two-thirds of the college's computers were replaced within six months.
The study found that today's refrigerators use less power than older models.
Nearly half of the town's streetlights stayed off on election day.
Tests suggest that newer engines are more likely to last than older ones.
Researchers compared how many apples and pears rot during shipping.
Only 12 percent of the district's buses passed the safety inspection.
The report shows that rural roads need more repairs than urban ones.
Tests suggest that most batteries lose charge within a year.

predictions: Fire 0.15-0.4, median ~0.22. Non-human statistic near misses ~0.02-0.1. AUROC ~0.9; median and AUROC are both at risk because the probes were weak and group nouns fired outside statistics too (0.14-0.29).
notes: Probes: 'the school's graduates went on to college' 0.41; 'The graduates threw their caps' 0.29 (no statistic); 'this decade's teenagers are less likely' 0.24; 'blacks in their area' 0.21; 'workers who speak out' 0.17; 'rural residents earn less' 0.17; 'age groups' 0.15; 'Some teenagers were playing' 0.14; floor 0.01. The pole seems to be about people-groups more than statistics, so near misses keep the statistic and swap the group of people for things.
